title: Questions about PCA
objectives: Explain what principal components are, how to choose how many, and when they mislead.

screens.title: The first component
screens.prose: About two minutes a question; say your reasoning aloud first. Three assets each have volatility 20%, and every pair correlates at 0.5. The chart shows the eigenvalues of their covariance matrix.
screens.question: What share of the total variance does the first component carry?

hints.text: The total variance is the sum of the eigenvalues.
That sum is the trace, $3 \times 0.04 = 0.12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the first eigenvalue by the sum of all three.

byKey.eig: That is the eigenvalue. The share divides it by the trace, 0.12.
byKey.third: That would hold if all three were equal.

explain.text: The share of a component is its eigenvalue over the trace. Here $0.08/0.12 = 66.67\%$: the common "market" move.

screens.title: Two components
screens.question: What share do the first two components carry together?

hints.text: Add the first two eigenvalues.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add two eigenvalues, then divide by the trace.

byKey.add: That is the sum of the two eigenvalues. Divide by the trace.

explain.text: Shares add: $(0.08 + 0.02)/0.12 = 83.33\%$. The last 0.02 is an equal split between two directions, so neither stands out.

screens.title: Units mislead
screens.prose: Two variables have variances 100 and 1, and covariance 9. So their correlation is $9/\sqrt{100 \times 1} = 0.9$. The covariance has eigenvalues 100.8115 and 0.1885; the correlation matrix has 1.9 and 0.1.

state.caption: The same two variables: covariance $\Sigma$ in raw units, correlation $R$ after scaling.

screens.question: Fill in the first component's share for each matrix.

hints.text: Each share is the top eigenvalue over the trace.
The traces are 101 and 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the top eigenvalue by each trace.

explain.text: On raw units the first component is 99.81% and points almost along $x_1$, the big-number variable. On correlations it is 95% and weighs both equally. Scale first unless the units mean something.

screens.title: Keep 90%?
screens.prose: Two standardised features correlate at 0.95. The target is their difference, $y = x_1 - x_2$. A candidate says: "Keep the components that explain 90%. That keeps the signal."

state.caption: 40 points with correlation 0.95. The target is $y = x_1 - x_2$.

screens.question: The first component explains 97.5% of the features. How much of $y$ does it explain?

options.text: None: $R^2 = 0$. The signal lives in the second component.
97.5%, its share of the variance of the features.
options.why: You used the share of the features' variance. That says nothing about $y$.

options.text: Most of it, since it is by far the bigger component.
options.why: Big in $x$ is not big in $y$. $y$ moves along the small direction.

options.text: Half, since there are two components and each takes a share.
options.why: Components are not split evenly for a target. Here one has all of it.

hints.text: Along which line does $x_1 - x_2$ change?
Moving along PC1, $x_1$ and $x_2$ rise together, so $x_1 - x_2$ stays put.
PC2 is exactly the direction of $x_1 - x_2$, so it carries all of $y$.

feedback.correct: PCA ranks by variance in $x$, not by relevance to $y$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask how $y$ changes along each line.

byKey.975: That is the trap: variance share is about the features. $y = x_1 - x_2$ is flat along PC1, so its $R^2$ there is 0.

explain.text: PCA never looks at the target. Here the 2.5% component carries all of $y$ ($R^2 = 1$) and the 97.5% one none. Dropping small components can drop the signal.

screens.title: Which sign is right?
screens.prose: Two runs of PCA on the same returns give two first components. Run 1 has loadings 0.58, 0.58, 0.58; run 2 has −0.58, −0.58, −0.58.
screens.question: Which run is right?

options.text: Both: an eigenvector and its negative describe the same direction.
Run 1: loadings on a common market move must be positive.
options.why: Nothing forces a sign. If $v$ is an eigenvector, so is $-v$.

options.text: Run 2: the later run replaces the first, so it is the current one.
options.why: Order of computing does not matter; both satisfy $\Sigma v = \lambda v$.

options.text: Neither: two runs on the same returns must agree, so one has a bug.
options.why: No bug: solvers pick a sign arbitrarily.

hints.text: Multiply $\Sigma v = \lambda v$ by −1.
$\Sigma(-v) = \lambda(-v)$.
So both signs are eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check whether $-v$ also solves $\Sigma v = \lambda v$.

explain.text: Eigenvectors are fixed only up to sign. Fix a convention, such as a positive sum of loadings, before you compare runs or trade a component.

screens.title: Noise has eigenvalues too
screens.prose: Pure noise, 2,000 rows and 1,000 columns. Every true eigenvalue is 1, yet the sample ones spread out. Theory puts the largest near $(1 + \sqrt{p/n})^2$.

state.caption: Seeded: $n = 2{,}000$ rows of pure noise, $p = 1{,}000$ columns. Largest eigenvalue 2.870.

screens.question: What is that edge for $p/n = 0.5$?

hints.text: Take the square root of 0.5 first.

byKey.one: Every true eigenvalue is 1, but sample eigenvalues spread out when $p$ is large against $n$.
byKey.noroot: You used $(1 + p/n)^2$. The edge has a square root inside.
byKey.sim: That is the seeded largest eigenvalue. The question asks for the theoretical edge.

explain.text: With $p/n = 0.5$ noise alone gives eigenvalues from about 0.086 to 2.914. A sample eigenvalue near 2.9 is not evidence of a factor.

screens.title: Say it aloud
screens.prose:
What you used:
$$\text{share}_k = \frac{\lambda_k}{\text{tr}\,\Sigma} = \frac{\lambda_k}{\sum_j \lambda_j}$$
Said aloud: "Principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance or correlation matrix. Each one's share is its eigenvalue over the trace. They rank directions by variance in the features, not by use for a target."
screens.question: Which answer would you give an interviewer?

options.text: "Eigenvectors of the covariance, or correlation if units differ. Share is eigenvalue over trace. They rank variance, not relevance to $y$."
"Eigenvectors of the covariance, chosen to predict the target best. Each share is how much of the target that component explains."
options.why: That is regression, or partial least squares. PCA never sees the target.

options.text: "Eigenvectors of the covariance, always of the raw data, since scaling loses information. Share is eigenvalue over trace."
options.why: On raw data the biggest units win, as with the 100 and 1 variances.

options.text: "Eigenvectors of the covariance; share is eigenvalue over trace. Keep components up to 90% and the signal is kept too."
options.why: The trap: a small component can carry the signal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the answer that also says what PCA ignores.

explain.text: A strong answer defines the components and says how to read a share. It also names the limit: PCA ranks variance, not relevance.

screens.title: Eigenvalues of a 2 by 2
screens.prose: Derive the eigenvalues 100.8115 and 0.1885 of $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 100 & 9 \\ 9 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ without a computer.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: The eigenvalues sum to the trace, $100 + 1 = 101$.
The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries, 100 and 1.
lines.why: That holds only for a diagonal matrix. The covariance 9 moves them apart.

hints.text: Use the trace and the determinant.
Sum 101, product 19.
Solve the quadratic with those.

feedback.correct: Trace and determinant give the quadratic.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Sum, product, quadratic, roots.

byKey.x: You read the diagonal. Off-diagonal terms change the eigenvalues.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step the derivation needs.

explain.text: For a 2 by 2, the eigenvalues have sum equal to the trace and product equal to the determinant. The quadratic gives 100.8115 and 0.1885, so the share is $100.8115/101 = 99.81\%$.

screens.title: The yield curve
screens.prose: Daily changes in 2, 5 and 10 year yields have standard deviations 5, 6 and 6 basis points. The eigenvalues of their covariance are 87.91, 7.49 and 1.60 bp².

state.caption: Daily changes, sd 5, 6, 6 bp. Correlations: 2y and 5y 0.9, 2y and 10y 0.75, 5y and 10y 0.9.

screens.question: What share of the variance is the first component?

hints.text: Divide by the trace.
The trace is $25 + 36 + 36 = 97$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the first eigenvalue by the trace, 97.

byKey.eig: That is the eigenvalue itself, in bp².
byKey.third: That would hold if all three were equal.

explain.text: The first component, with loadings near 0.49, 0.63, 0.61, is a parallel shift: 90.63%. The second, about 0.71, 0.12, −0.70, is the slope, 7.72%.

screens.title: The follow-up
screens.prose: The interviewer asks: "How many components do you keep, and why?"

state.caption: Daily changes, sd 5, 6, 6 bp. Correlations: 2y and 5y 0.9, 2y and 10y 0.75, 5y and 10y 0.9.

screens.question: Which answer would you give?

options.text: "To describe, those above the noise edge. To predict, as many as do best out of sample, small ones included."
"Enough to reach 90% of the variance. The rest is small, so it is mostly noise and safe to drop."
options.why: A fixed share ignores noise and the target. The trap showed a 2.5% component can carry all of $y$.

options.text: "Always one: the market. Every other component is noise around the common move of the curve."
options.why: The second and third components here are slope and curvature, which desks hedge.

options.text: "All of them, so nothing is lost. Dropping a component throws away variance that we paid to measure."
options.why: Then PCA has reduced nothing, and noise components add variance.

hints.text: Separate describing the data from predicting a target.
Noise sets an edge for eigenvalues.
For a target, judge each component by held-out error.

feedback.correct: It depends on the job: noise edge to describe, held-out error to predict.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Pick the answer that names a test, not a fixed share.

explain.text: Compare eigenvalues with what noise alone would give, as with the 2.914 edge. If there is a target, choose by out-of-sample error, since a small component can carry it.

ideas: Components are eigenvectors of the covariance (or correlation) matrix; a share is eigenvalue over trace.
Raw units let the biggest variable win; scale first unless units mean something.
PCA ranks variance in the features, not use for a target: a small component can hold the signal.
summary.trap: Keeping the components that explain 90% does not keep the signal: PCA never sees the target.

quiz.prose: Two assets with equal volatility 30% and correlation 0.6.
quiz.question: What share does the first component carry?

byKey.half: That holds only at zero correlation.

explain.text: With equal variances the eigenvalues are $\sigma^2(1 + \rho)$ and $\sigma^2(1 - \rho)$. The share is $(1 + 0.6)/2 = 0.8$.

quiz.question: What share does the first component of the correlation matrix carry?

feedback.generic: Not quite. The larger eigenvalue is $1 + |\rho|$.

byKey.neg: You took $1 + \rho = 0.6$ as the top. With $\rho < 0$ the top is $1 - \rho = 1.4$.

explain.text: The eigenvalues are $1 \pm \rho$: 1.4 and 0.6. The first component is $(1, -1)/\sqrt{2}$ and carries 70%.

quiz.question: Near what value is the largest sample eigenvalue?

byKey.one: True eigenvalues are 1; sample ones spread.

explain.text: The edge is $(1 + \sqrt{p/n})^2 = 1.5^2 = 2.25$. Eigenvalues below it are what noise alone produces.

quiz.prose: You run PCA on a price in pence and a volume in shares, both raw.
quiz.question: What will the first component mostly be?

options.text: Whichever variable has the bigger raw variance.
The common move of both, as with correlated returns.
options.why: That needs comparable scales. On raw data the big-variance column dominates.

options.text: The price, since it is the variable that matters more.
options.why: PCA does not know what matters; it follows variance.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what PCA maximises.

explain.text: PCA maximises variance, so the column with the biggest numbers wins. Standardise first to use correlations.
